paths/why-the-reformation-happened/summa: Not one cause but many: a weakened papacy, earlier reform movements, humanism and printing, the indulgence controversy, rival theologies of grace and the sacraments, and princes who saw their chance.
paths/why-the-reformation-happened/steps: A papacy in crisis

The popes' residence at Avignon (1309-77) and then the Great Western Schism (1378-1417), when two and then three rival popes claimed authority, damaged papal prestige and encouraged conciliarism, the idea that general councils stand above popes.
Forerunners: Waldensians, Wycliffe and Hus

Long before Luther, the Waldensians preached apostolic poverty and vernacular Scripture; John Wycliffe attacked papal power and transubstantiation; Jan Hus in Prague called for reform and was burned at the Council of Constance in 1415 despite a safe-conduct. Hussite churches survived in Bohemia.
Humanism and the printing press

Renaissance humanists cried 'ad fontes' (back to the sources). Erasmus published the Greek New Testament in 1516 and satirised clerical abuses. Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1450) meant reformers' pamphlets could spread across Europe within weeks.
Indulgences and the 95 Theses

Johann Tetzel's preaching of an indulgence to fund St Peter's in Rome provoked the Augustinian friar and professor Martin Luther to issue 95 theses for debate (31 October 1517). Behind the protest lay Luther's discovery, through Romans, of justification as a gift received by faith rather than earned by penance.
Worms: Scripture and conscience

Excommunicated in 1521, Luther refused to recant before Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason. Protected by Frederick the Wise of Saxony, he translated the New Testament into German, making Scripture's authority over church tradition a defining issue.
Zurich and the Supper

In Zurich Huldrych Zwingli led an independent, more radical reform of worship. At the Marburg Colloquy (1529) Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles but split over Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper, dividing Protestantism into Lutheran and Reformed streams.
The Radical Reformation

Some of Zwingli's followers, including Conrad Grebel, concluded that baptism belongs only to confessing believers and that the church must be separate from the state. Their adult baptisms in January 1525 began the Anabaptist movement, persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike.
Princes, kings and politics

The Reformation succeeded where rulers backed it. Lutheran princes presented the Augsburg Confession (1530); Henry VIII broke with Rome through the Act of Supremacy (1534), largely over his marriage; the Peace of Augsburg (1555) let each German ruler choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his territory.
Calvin and an international Reformed movement

John Calvin's Institutes (final edition 1559) and his Geneva Academy trained pastors for France, the Netherlands, Scotland and beyond, making Reformed Protestantism an international movement with presbyterian church order.
Catholic Reform and the long aftermath

The Council of Trent (1545-63) answered Protestant teaching on Scripture, justification and the sacraments while reforming clerical discipline; new orders such as Ignatius of Loyola's Jesuits renewed Catholic education and mission. Religious wars followed until the Peace of Westphalia (1648).
paths/why-the-reformation-happened/quiz/: What immediately provoked Luther's 95 Theses in 1517?
The preaching of an indulgence to fund St Peter's in Rome
Johann Tetzel's indulgence campaign, partly funding the rebuilding of St Peter's Basilica, prompted the theses.
Which reformer was burned at the Council of Constance in 1415?
Jan Hus was condemned and burned at Constance; Wycliffe died in 1384 and his remains were later exhumed and burned.
What was the main disagreement at the Marburg Colloquy (1529)?
Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper
Luther and Zwingli disagreed on whether Christ's body is truly present in the bread and wine.
What did the first Anabaptists do in Zurich in January 1525?
Baptised one another as confessing adults
Conrad Grebel baptised George Blaurock, who then baptised others, rejecting infant baptism.
The principle later summarised as 'cuius regio, eius religio' comes from...
The Peace of Augsburg allowed each ruler in the Empire to choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his lands; the Latin tag was coined later.
Who published the first printed Greek New Testament in 1516?
Erasmus' Novum Instrumentum (1516) fed the humanist return to the sources that Luther used.
Which council was the main Catholic response to the Reformation?
The Council of Trent met in three periods between 1545 and 1563.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/summary: Is salvation chiefly a courtroom verdict, a sharing in God's own life, or both? Trace the 'legal' (forensic) and 'union' (participatory) ways of telling the gospel from the New Testament to today's debates, with each side in its best light.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/0/tit: Two vocabularies in the New Testament
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/0/tex: Paul speaks both of justification (a legal verdict: Romans 3-5) and of being 'in Christ', crucified and raised with him (Galatians 2:20; Romans 6); John speaks of abiding in Christ (John 15), and 2 Peter 1:4 of becoming 'partakers of the divine nature'. Every later tradition draws on both, but weights them differently.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/1/tex: Irenaeus taught that Christ 'recapitulates' (sums up) the human story, undoing Adam's disobedience by his obedience, so that humanity can grow into God's likeness. Salvation here is the healing and maturing of the human race in union with the incarnate Son.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/2/tex: In On the Incarnation Athanasius argued that the Word became human so that humans might be made divine (ch. 54) and that his death paid the debt and defeated corruption and death. Eastern Christianity built on this the doctrine of theosis.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/3/tex: Augustine's battle with Pelagius made grace, original sin and guilt central in the West. Latin theology, shaped also by Tertullian's legal vocabulary, increasingly framed salvation in terms of sin, debt, merit and justice, though Augustine also wrote richly of union with Christ.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/4/tex: Anselm's Cur Deus Homo argued that sin dishonours God and that only a God-man could offer the satisfaction humanity owes. Abelard replied that the cross chiefly reveals love that awakens love. These became the poles of medieval Western atonement theory.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/5/tex: In the East, Gregory Palamas defended the hesychasts' claim to see the uncreated light: humans truly participate in God's energies while God's essence remains beyond them. For Orthodoxy this secured real union with God without pantheism.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/6/tit: Luther and Calvin: verdict and union
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/6/tex: Luther taught justification by faith alone through the imputed righteousness of Christ, and also a 'joyful exchange' in which Christ and the believer share all things. Calvin's Institutes (1559) made union with Christ the source of a 'double grace': justification and sanctification.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/7/tit: Federal theology and the courtroom gospel
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/7/tex: Reformed 'federal' (covenant) theology, codified in the Westminster Confession, framed history as a covenant of works with Adam and a covenant of grace in Christ, the last Adam, who bears the penalty for sin. Penal substitution became central to much evangelical preaching.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/8/tit: Scottish dissent: McLeod Campbell and the Torrances
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/8/tex: John McLeod Campbell, deposed in 1831 for teaching that Christ died for all, argued in The Nature of the Atonement (1856) that Christ offered a perfect 'amen' of repentance and sonship on our behalf. In the 20th century T.F. and J.B. Torrance contrasted 'covenant' with 'contract' and stressed Christ's vicarious humanity; Gustaf Aulén's Christus Victor (1931) revived the patristic victory motif.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/steps/9/tex: Writers such as C. Baxter Kruger and François du Toit press a strongly incarnational 'union' gospel in which humanity is already included in Christ, while defenders of penal substitution such as J.I. Packer and John Piper argue that the legal dimension is non-negotiable. Others, like N.T. Wright, reframe justification around covenant membership. Compare the positions side by side in the Legal vs Union comparison.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/0/ques: Which work by Anselm set out the satisfaction theory of atonement?
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/0/expl: Cur Deus Homo ('Why God Became Man', 1098) argues that only a God-man could make satisfaction for human sin.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/1/ques: Who wrote that the Word 'became man that we might be made God'?
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/1/expl: Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54, a foundational text for the doctrine of theosis.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/2/ques: What did Calvin call the twofold benefit received through union with Christ?
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/2/expl: For Calvin, union with Christ yields the 'double grace' of justification and sanctification (Institutes 3.11.1).
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/3/ques: Why was John McLeod Campbell deposed from the Church of Scotland ministry in 1831?
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/3/opti: For teaching that Christ died for all and that assurance belongs to faith
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/3/expl: The General Assembly judged his teaching on universal atonement and assurance contrary to the Westminster Confession.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/4/ques: Gustaf Aulén's 1931 book revived which view of the atonement?
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/4/expl: Aulén argued that the early church's dominant view was Christ's victory over sin, death and the devil.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/5/ques: James B. Torrance contrasted the biblical idea of covenant with what?
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/5/expl: Torrance argued that federal theology tended to turn God's unconditional covenant of grace into a conditional contract.
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/6/ques: Which theologian is most associated with the defence of hesychast experience of the uncreated light?
paths/legal-vs-union-gospels/quiz/6/expl: Gregory Palamas' Triads (1338-41) defended the hesychasts; councils at Constantinople upheld his teaching (1341-51).
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/summary: How a movement that began in small prayer meetings in 1901-1906 came to number hundreds of millions: its roots in Acts, earlier prophetic and revival movements, Methodism and the Holiness movement, and its many birthplaces around the world.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/steps/0/te: Pentecostals read Acts 2 not only as history but as a pattern: the disciples were 'filled with the Holy Ghost' and spoke in tongues. Joel's promise that God would pour out his Spirit 'on all flesh' became a key text of the movement.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/steps/1/te: Prophecy continued in the second century, but the Montanist 'New Prophecy' and its ecstatic oracles led the wider church to test prophecy by apostolic teaching and episcopal oversight. Pentecostal historians often cite this as the moment charismatic gifts receded from the mainstream.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/steps/2/te: German Pietism stressed new birth and heart religion. The Moravian community at Herrnhut experienced a communal outpouring in August 1727 and began a round-the-clock prayer watch and worldwide missions.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/steps/3/te: John Wesley's heart was 'strangely warmed' at Aldersgate. His teaching on assurance and on 'Christian perfection' (entire sanctification) as a second work of grace after conversion became the theological seed of the 'second blessing' idea.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/steps/4/te: The Cane Ridge meeting in Kentucky (1801) and the Second Great Awakening spread an American revival culture of camp meetings, falling, shouting and immediate decision; Charles Finney later systematised 'new measures' for revival.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/steps/5/te: Phoebe Palmer's 'altar theology' taught that entire sanctification could be received instantly by consecration and faith. By the late 19th century many Holiness preachers called this a 'baptism of the Holy Ghost' empowering believers, alongside a growing divine healing movement and expectation of Christ's imminent return.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/steps/6/te: At Charles Parham's Bethel Bible School in Topeka, Agnes Ozman spoke in tongues on 1 January 1901. Parham taught that tongues were the 'Bible evidence' of Spirit baptism, giving Pentecostalism its distinctive doctrine.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/steps/7/te: Revival swept Wales under Evan Roberts (1904-05), the Mukti Mission of Pandita Ramabai in India (1905) and Pyongyang in Korea (1907). News travelled through missionary periodicals, so Pentecostalism had several origins, not only an American one.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/steps/8/te: William J. Seymour's interracial mission at 312 Azusa Street, Los Angeles (1906-09) became the movement's most famous centre, sending missionaries worldwide. Disputes soon followed: over race, over sanctification (Finished Work, 1910) and over the Trinity, which produced Oneness Pentecostalism (1913-16). The Assemblies of God formed in 1914.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/steps/9/ti: Charismatic renewal and the global South
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/steps/9/te: From 1960 Pentecostal experience entered mainline Protestant and, from 1967, Catholic churches (the Charismatic Renewal), while independent 'neo-charismatic' and African, Latin American and Asian churches grew rapidly. By the early 21st century Pentecostal and charismatic Christians were estimated at roughly a quarter of all Christians, most in the global South.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/0/que: Who led the Azusa Street Mission in Los Angeles from 1906?
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/0/exp: Seymour, an African American Holiness preacher and former student of Parham, led the mission.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/1/que: Where did Agnes Ozman speak in tongues on 1 January 1901?
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/1/exp: At Charles Parham's Bethel Bible School in Topeka.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/2/que: Classical Pentecostals teach that the 'initial physical evidence' of Spirit baptism is...
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/2/exp: The 'initial evidence' doctrine, formulated by Parham, became standard in groups such as the Assemblies of God.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/3/que: Which Wesleyan teaching paved the way for the idea of a 'second blessing'?
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/3/exp: Wesley's teaching on Christian perfection as a distinct work of grace was developed by the Holiness movement into an instantaneous 'second blessing'.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/4/que: Who led the revival at the Mukti Mission in India in 1905?
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/4/exp: Pandita Ramabai's mission for widows and orphans at Kedgaon experienced revival from June 1905.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/5/que: Oneness Pentecostalism, which emerged around 1913-16, differs from most Pentecostals by...
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/5/opt: Rejecting the doctrine of the Trinity and baptising in Jesus' name only
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/5/exp: Oneness Pentecostals reject classical Trinitarianism, placing them outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/6/que: Whose 'altar theology' taught instantaneous entire sanctification by consecration and faith?
paths/roots-of-pentecostalism/quiz/6/exp: Phoebe Palmer's teaching (The Way of Holiness, 1843) shaped the Holiness movement.
